open-question.question: No scenario invocation carries a time or turn limit while the rater has one, so a runaway session can hold a run open indefinitely. Does each invocation get a time or turn limit, and how is an invocation that hits it classified?
open-question.alternative: Two generous limits per claude -p process, both declared as shared inputs of the comparison set. The first is a host-enforced spend or turn cap; reaching it is a behavioural early stop, recorded and rated on the tree left. The second is a harness wall-clock ceiling set above anything the spend cap allows in normal operation; a kill there is classified as an infrastructure failure and handled by the infrastructure-failure policy. The manifest records which limit ended the invocation. Sorts the two ways a session runs away by mechanism, not by judgment: a model that keeps working hits the spend cap and is scored, and a session that stalls hits the clock and is not. This bounds every run without scoring outside slowdowns against a scenario. Two parameters to set, declare, and justify instead of one, plus a dependence on a host flag whose coverage of subagents must be confirmed. Handling of the clock hit depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

Scenario invocations keep running with no time, turn, or spend limit, per invocation or per run, as the draft's one-run procedure now stands. A session ends only by itself or by a failed call, its wall-clock duration is recorded in the manifest as today, and no limit-hit end class exists. Adds no parameter to the design and cuts no scenario short. A slow invocation, most likely Cairn's long task-completion line, can never be stopped by a ceiling set too low, so no score depends on where the ceiling was set. A runaway or hung session holds its run, and any campaign waiting behind it, open indefinitely. The only way to end it is a person killing the process, which breaks the draft's rule that nothing about a run is done by hand, and the kill leaves an end that no rule classifies.

The harness kills each claude -p process after a fixed wall-clock ceiling. This covers the first-form invocation and each operator-reply resume, each process timed on its own. The ceiling is set generously, well above the longest normal invocation (for example a stated multiple of a pilot's longest), and declared as a shared input of the comparison set. A kill stops the chain and is recorded in the manifest as its own end class (time limit). The run is then scored like any other early stop: a result, rated on the tree it left. Bounds every run with one harness-side mechanism that needs no host flag and catches hangs as well as loops. It rarely binds, so it does not shape scores, and it fits the draft's existing rule that an early stop is a result, not a failed measurement. Wall-clock time also depends on API speed and the network, so a hit can come from a stalled connection rather than the model, and counting it as a result scores an outside slowdown against the scenario. Cairn's long invocations are the most exposed to this.

The same generous per-process wall-clock ceiling, declared as a shared input of the comparison set and enforced by the harness, but a kill is classified as an infrastructure failure, not a behavioural stop. It is recorded under that end class and handled by whatever the benchmark does with infrastructure failures, so it is not scored as the scenario's result. A scenario is not penalised for a session held open by something outside the model, such as a stalled API or network. That keeps the bias the gaps report raises (Cairn, the heaviest spender, being the likeliest to hit external limits) out of the scores. A genuine model runaway, such as a loop that never converges, also gets treated as an infrastructure failure, which hides a real behavioural failure mode and can reward it with a retry. What a hit costs depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

alternative.id: Spend or turn cap as result

open-question.alternative: Each invocation runs under a fixed cap the host enforces in the model's own terms: a dollar budget (claude -p's --max-budget-usd) or a cap on agentic turns where the host offers one. The cap is set generously and declared as a shared input of the comparison set, and there is no wall-clock ceiling. Reaching the cap is a behavioural early stop, recorded in the manifest under a limit end class and rated on the tree left. A cap counted in spend or turns does not depend on API or network speed, so a hit always reflects what the model did. Classifying it as a result is then sound. It is also one parameter that is easy to state and to reproduce. It does not bound a hang that spends nothing, such as a stalled connection or a blocked tool call, so the indefinitely-open run the question raises remains possible. It also depends on a host flag whose scope over dispatched subagents must be confirmed, and that flag is recorded per host rather than enforced by the harness.

A deliberately tight per-invocation limit, in time or spend, that is the same for every scenario and chosen to bind rather than to catch only runaways. Reaching it is an early stop rated on the tree left, so the benchmark measures quality reached within a fixed resource budget. Answers the question of which approach does best when given the same resources, a comparison a reader can take at face value without weighing cost separately. Turns the cost the draft reports beside quality into a constraint on quality. The draft states that Cairn is expected to cost more and that the benchmark reports by how much, so this would systematically cut Cairn's heaviest lines short and score that against it, and the scores would then depend on where the budget was set.

A single wall-clock ceiling on the whole run (every invocation, reply, and operator turn of one prompt's chain), declared as a shared input of the comparison set, with no per-invocation limit. When the deadline passes the harness kills the running process and stops the chain. The run is recorded with a deadline end class and rated on the tree left as an early stop. One number bounds every run's total duration, and with it the length of a campaign, without having to size a ceiling for each kind of invocation. Chains differ greatly in length, from the single manual message to Cairn's eleven or more lines, so one deadline either binds Cairn or is slack for manual. It also lets a runaway early invocation use up the time of every later line, so the stop shows up at a line that did nothing wrong.

open-question.question: The ranking-table section opens by saying the table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches, while the radar text says the page states no claim the data does not. Does that sentence change to say the table shows whether Cairn beats them?
open-question.recommendation: The results section then carries one explicitly falsifiable hypothesis in the style the phase-2 paragraph already uses, naming in advance the table and the curve that would refute it, which is a stronger honesty commitment than a bare whether and consistent across both parts.
open-question.alternative: The table's opener is recast as the refutable expectation described for the table-only expectation option, with the purpose sentence folded in. The radar's opening is recast the same way: it is where the expected gain is located by axis, its curves are drawn whatever they show, and a Cairn curve inside a manual one refutes the expectation on that axis. The radar's existing list of axes where the gain is expected stays as the stated expectation. The whole results section carries one consistent, explicitly falsifiable hypothesis, the same framing the phase-2 paragraph uses. A reader sees both what was predicted and that a contrary result is shown, in the table and the chart alike. It rewrites the most prose, including radar text beside the curve-selection reasoning a sibling question may also change (a condition on that radar curve choice). Like the table-only expectation, it keeps the author's expected outcome at the head of each part.

The opening sentence of "The ranking table" in ideas/benchmark_for_cairn.md stays as written ("The table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches as a family of configurations, not as one tuned winner"). No other sentence of the table or radar sections changes, and the draft records that the sentence was kept, with the reason, as the resolution of gap 18. It states plainly the result the benchmark was built to show. The radar's rule that the page states no claim the curves do not is about the generated page, not about this design prose, so the two need not conflict, and the draft is not edited at all. The draft would assert a result before any run exists. That contradicts its own refutable framing at the phase-2 expectation and in the radar text, and it is exactly the inconsistency the gaps report flags. It also reads as a benchmark designed to confirm its author's product, which weakens the "proof of whether Cairn helps" purpose stated in the general idea.

Only the opening sentence changes, from "shows that Cairn beats" to "shows whether Cairn beats the other approaches as a family of configurations, not as one tuned winner". The rest of the table section stays as written, including "The reading it exists to give is several Cairn rows … standing above the best manual row", and the radar section stays as written. It is the smallest edit that removes the contradiction the gaps report names. It is the report's own fix, word for word, and it leaves the "family of configurations" framing that justifies listing every Cairn row. The purpose sentence a few lines later still describes Cairn rows above the best manual row as the reading the table exists to give, with no counterpart for a table where they stand below. The radar still opens with "how much better, and where", so the section would ask "whether" and then assume the answer.

The opening sentence changes to "shows whether Cairn beats …", and the table section's purpose sentence is reworded to match: several Cairn rows standing above the best manual row becomes the reading the table is built to make visible if it holds, and a table where they stand below is published in the same form. The radar section stays as written. The whole ranking-table section then reads as neutral, opener and purpose sentence alike. It keeps the reason every Cairn configuration appears, losers included, and leaves the radar text, which already says it draws whatever the data shows, untouched. The radar's opening line "The radar shows how much better, and where" still assumes a margin exists, so the results section stays neutral in one half and presumptive in the other.

The table's opener and purpose sentence change as in the table-section rewording ("whether", and a losing table published in the same form). The radar's opening line also changes from "how much better, and where" to a neutral form saying whether the Cairn curves sit outside the manual ones, by how much, and on which axes. The rest of the radar text is unchanged, including its no-claim rule and the reasoning behind which curves are drawn. Every sentence that introduces a part of the results section then states a question rather than an answer, which matches the radar's existing "the page states no claim the curves do not" rule and makes the whole page consistent with it. It is the largest of the "whether" edits and reaches into radar prose next to the curve-selection reasoning. If that reasoning is rewritten separately, the two edits touch the same paragraph and must be kept consistent (a condition on the radar curve choice, which a sibling question owns).

The opening sentence is recast as a refutable expectation instead of a neutral question, in the style of the draft's phase-2 paragraph. The table is where the benchmark expects several Cairn rows, under different versions and model strategies, to stand above the best manual row, and a table in which they do not refutes that expectation and is published all the same. The purpose sentence is folded into this statement. The radar section stays as written. It keeps the benchmark's hypothesis on the page explicitly, which a bare "whether" drops, and names in advance the result that would refute it. That is a stronger honesty commitment than neutrality, and it matches how the draft already treats phase 2. It still leads with the outcome the author expects, which a reader may take as advocacy. The radar's "how much better, and where" stays presumptive, so the expectation is stated as refutable for the table but not for the chart beside it.

The opening sentence is removed rather than reworded, and the table section opens with what the table is: one row per rated configuration of the four primary deliveries, ordered by rank. The purpose sentence keeps only its rule that every rated Cairn configuration appears, losers included, without describing which reading is expected. The radar section stays as written. The table section then makes no claim and states no hypothesis, so nothing in it can contradict the radar's no-claim rule. It describes only what the analysis generates, which is all an implementer of the table needs. The README introduction says the table and the radar "answer two different questions", and this would leave the table's question unstated. The reason Cairn is shown as a family of configurations rather than one tuned winner also loses its stated motivation.

open-question.question: The rank orders scenarios by overall score and breaks ties by cost, with no threshold below which two scores count as equal, so a difference within noise still orders two rows. Is there a margin under which two overall scores tie and cost decides?
open-question.recommendation: Rows are ordered only where the set's own per-run ranges separate them and tied rows share a rank, so the headline reading is claimed only when the data supports it, no constant has to be argued for, and cost stays unranked as the draft states.
open-question.alternative: The margin is derived per comparison set from the set's own measured noise, by a declared statistical bound on the difference of two scenarios' per-run overall scores (for example overlapping intervals at a declared level, widened by the rater agreement figure where one is reported); scenarios within it of their group's top row share one rank number and are marked as tied, and cost plays no part in the rank. The most defensible statement the page can make: rows are ordered only where the set's own data separates them, and the benchmark never weighs cost against quality for the reader. Depends on several runs per scenario and a computed spread, owned by the Runs per scenario and Score spread reporting questions; it carries the most analysis machinery, the threshold varies between comparison sets, and with few runs most rows may tie, leaving the table's headline reading and the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" (the Radar curve selection question) without a clear order.

The rank stays as the draft has it: scenarios are ordered by the exact overall score, only two exactly equal scores tie, and cost breaks such a tie in favour of the cheaper scenario. No margin is declared, and whether a margin between two rows is noise is left to whatever the table reports beside the scores. Nothing new to define, justify, or keep in step: the rank is a total order computed mechanically from the per-axis means, with no constant anyone has to argue for and no grouping rule for chains of near-equal scores. Overall scores are means of fractions, so exact equality practically never occurs and the cost rule is dead text; a difference well inside noise still orders two rows, so the table's intended reading (Cairn rows above the best manual row) can rest on noise, and a reader can tell otherwise only if the table reports a spread, which the Score spread reporting question owns.

Overall scores are compared at the precision the table prints them (for example whole points on the 0 to 100 scale): two scores that print the same tie, and the cheaper scenario ranks higher. No noise-based margin is declared. The rank never contradicts what the reader sees, since two rows showing the same overall are never ordered by an invisible decimal, and the existing cost rule becomes live without introducing a tuned constant. Print precision is a formatting choice, not a noise estimate: differences of a few points, which can still be rater or run noise, keep ordering rows, so the gap the question raises is narrowed only at its smallest end.

Overall scores are compared at the precision the table prints them: two scores that print the same share one rank number and are marked as tied, and their listing order within the tie carries no claim (cost no longer breaks ties). No noise-based margin is declared. Removes the contradiction between the draft's rule that cost is never ranked and its use of cost as a tie-breaker, while keeping the rank consistent with what is printed and adding no constant. Like the other print-precision option it leaves noise-sized differences ordering rows; and a shared top rank within a family leaves the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" ambiguous, which needs a rule from the Radar curve selection question.

The draft declares one fixed margin in points on the 0 to 100 overall score, set before a comparison set's first scored run and versioned with the analysis; two scenarios whose overall scores differ by less than it tie, and the cheaper one ranks higher. Tie groups are formed from the top of the order down, each row joining the group whose top row it is within the margin of, so chains of near-equal scores resolve one way. A quality difference too small to trust can no longer put an expensive scenario above a cheaper one, which is the reading the cost tie-break was written for; the rule is simple, reproducible from the columns, and identical across comparison sets, so ranks under it compare over the trend. The margin's value is chosen before any noise has been measured, so it is a guess that may be too tight to matter or too loose to separate real differences; it brings cost into the rank, against the draft's statement that cost is never ranked, and can lift a cheap manual row above a Cairn row on the page's headline reading.

The draft declares one fixed margin in points on the 0 to 100 overall score, set before a comparison set's first scored run and versioned with the analysis; scenarios whose overall scores fall within it of their group's top row share one rank number and are marked as tied, and cost plays no part in the rank, staying a column the reader weighs. Says exactly what the data supports, that the tied rows are indistinguishable on quality, without the benchmark weighing cost for the reader, which keeps the rank consistent with the draft's rule that cost is never ranked. The margin is still a guess made before noise is measured; tied groups make the table's ordering partly uninformative, and the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" becomes ambiguous within a tied group, which needs a rule from the Radar curve selection question.

The margin is not a constant but is derived per comparison set from the set's own measured noise: two scenarios tie when the difference between their overall scores lies within a declared statistical bound computed from their per-run scores (for example overlapping intervals at a declared level, widened by the rater agreement figure where one is reported), and within a tie the cheaper scenario ranks higher. The bound's formula and level are declared in the draft before the first scored run. A tie means precisely "this difference is within the noise the set actually showed", so the rank tracks the data rather than a guessed constant, and cost decides only where quality genuinely cannot. It exists only if the set carries several runs per scenario and computes a per-run spread, axes owned by the Runs per scenario and Score spread reporting questions (with one run per scenario no bound can be computed); the analysis grows more complex, the threshold moves between comparison sets so ranks are not formed under one rule over the trend, and cost enters the rank against the draft's statement that it is never ranked.

open-question.question: The hidden-requirements axis rests on two checks per run (one reading line in phase 1 and one test line in phase 2) yet weighs one third of the overall score, as much as roughly thirty-seven implied lines. Does the hidden axis keep equal weight in the overall score, or is it reported beside an overall computed without it?
open-question.recommendation: The hidden axis is the outcome the benchmark exists to test, so it keeps full influence on the rank, with the per-axis columns and ranges beside the overall and the measured tie rule absorbing the two-check noise as ties rather than a weight burying the signal.
open-question.alternative: The overall score stays the unweighted mean of the stated, hidden, and implied axes, and the rank still orders by it. The hidden requirement stays one per prompt, so the axis keeps resting on the phase-1 reading line (a count out of ten) and the phase-2 yes-or-no test line. The draft adds the reason the hidden axis keeps its third despite its two checks, and the ranking table keeps the per-axis columns beside the overall as it does now. It keeps the draft's stated rule that equal weights are the only weights nobody has to argue for, and leaves the axis the question-and-answer loop is tested on at full influence on the rank, where the draft expects Cairn's gain to show. Two checks per run carry as much of the overall as about thirty-seven implied lines, and the phase-2 check is binary, so one run's 0 or 100 on a single test moves the overall by a third of the scale and can reorder the rank on noise; the draft would be keeping, knowingly, the imbalance the design-gaps report raised.

The overall score becomes the unweighted mean of the stated and implied axes only, and the rank orders by that. The hidden axis stays a scored axis in every other place: its own ranking-table column beside the overall, and its axis on the radar. The draft states why the hidden axis is reported beside the rank rather than in it. The rank no longer swings on two checks, and the hidden result is still shown on its own, unblended, where a reader sees the clearest evidence the benchmark produces without it being diluted or amplified by a weighting choice. The one axis designed to show what Cairn's question loop buys stops affecting the rank, so a scenario that never meets a hidden requirement can rank first, and the headline ordering no longer reflects the outcome the benchmark exists to test; a reader must read two numbers to see the comparison the draft frames as its point.

The hidden axis stays in the overall score but at a declared weight below the other two (for example half the weight of each), the overall becoming a weighted mean whose weights the draft states and fixes per comparison set. The hidden column and radar axis stay as they are. The hidden result still bears on the rank, so a scenario that surfaces the hidden requirement is rewarded, while one noisy binary check can no longer move the overall by a full third of the scale. Any weight below a third and above zero is a number someone has to argue for, the very thing the draft's equal-weight rule avoids, and the chosen value is arbitrary with no line-count or evidential basis to anchor it; a later change to it is an analysis version that splits comparisons made before and after it.

The overall score stops being a mean of axis scores and becomes the passing share of every checklist line pooled across axes, each line counting once (a reading line contributing its items' fraction), so each axis weighs in proportion to how many lines it has: the hidden axis about two lines' worth across both prompts, the stated axis its sentences, and the implied axis its roughly thirty-seven lines. The per-axis scores stay in their columns and on the radar. The weights follow mechanically from the checklist with nothing chosen by hand, so each check counts the same and the overall's sensitivity to any one check matches the evidence behind it. It also reweights the stated axis, which the draft calls the floor under the others, down to a handful of lines against the implied list, so the overall becomes mostly an implied-coverage score; the hidden result all but vanishes from the rank, and every later change to an implied list's length silently shifts every axis's weight.

Equal weight is kept, and the premise that the axis rests on two checks is rejected instead: the "one per prompt" rule is replaced by a fixed number of hidden requirements per prompt (several, each with its own seed evidence and check line), so the hidden axis becomes the mean over several checks per prompt like the other axes. It removes the imbalance at its cause rather than by weighting: the axis that tests the question loop keeps its third of the rank while resting on enough checks that one missed requirement no longer swings it. Each extra hidden requirement needs seed evidence calibrated so the prompt gives no reason to ask yet the question settles it, in a small seed README where several planted pieces of evidence can point at each other or at an implied convention; it multiplies the authoring and calibration work, changes the seed and the Closest Wins project section, and depends on whatever calibration procedure the hidden-requirement pilot sets.

The overall score and the rank are dropped: the ranking table shows the three axis scores side by side with no blended number, ordered by a fixed key the draft states (such as delivery family then scenario id), and the radar stays the per-axis comparison. No weight for the hidden axis, or any axis, is set because no axes are combined. No weighting question exists at all, so nothing about the hidden axis's two checks is amplified or buried, and the page shows only numbers each re-derivable from the checklist lines, consistent with the draft's refusal to weigh trade-offs for the reader. The page loses its one-glance answer to which approach is best and the table's reason to order its rows, and the radar's per-family curve is currently chosen by rank, so this depends on how the radar curve selection is settled; the tie-by-cost rule and the "several Cairn rows above the best manual row" reading lose their basis.
